questions.questionText: Which of the following substances consists of a giant covalent lattice?
options: Silicon dioxide ($SiO_2$)
Carbon dioxide ($CO_2$)
Sodium chloride ($NaCl$)
Magnesium oxide ($MgO$)
questions.correctAnswer: Silicon dioxide ($SiO_2$)

solution.formulaSetup: Classification of chemical structures: simple molecular vs giant covalent vs giant ionic.
steps: $SiO_2$ has a giant covalent macromolecular structure where every silicon atom is covalently bonded to 4 oxygen atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement.
$CO_2$ is simple covalent molecular (individual molecules held by weak intermolecular forces).
$NaCl$ and $MgO$ are giant ionic lattices held by electrostatic attraction between ions.
solution.finalAnswer: Silicon dioxide ($SiO_2$)
solution.commonTrap: Confusing $SiO_2$ with $CO_2$ because carbon and silicon are in the same Group 14.

questions.questionText: Why does molten potassium chloride ($KCl$) conduct electricity, whereas solid $KCl$ does not?
options: Potassium and chloride ions become mobile in the molten state
Electrons become delocalised in the liquid state
Molecules can rotate freely when melted
Potassium metal is produced upon heating
questions.correctAnswer: Potassium and chloride ions become mobile in the molten state

solution.formulaSetup: Electrical conductivity requires mobile charge carriers (delocalised electrons or mobile ions).
steps: In solid $KCl$, $K^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions are held in fixed positions within the giant ionic lattice by strong electrostatic forces, so they cannot move.
When melted into liquid state, the ionic lattice breaks down, allowing the ions to become mobile and act as charge carriers.
Note: Ionic compounds NEVER conduct via mobile electrons (electrons remain tightly held by ions).
solution.finalAnswer: Potassium and chloride ions become mobile in the molten state
solution.commonTrap: Claiming that 'delocalised electrons conduct electricity in molten salts', which loses the mark immediately.

questions.questionText: Why does graphite conduct electricity along its layers, whereas diamond is an electrical insulator?
options: Each carbon in graphite forms 3 covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom
Graphite contains mobile carbon ions
Graphite is an ionic compound
Diamond has weak intermolecular forces that block electrons
questions.correctAnswer: Each carbon in graphite forms 3 covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom

solution.formulaSetup: Structure-property relationship of carbon allotropes.
steps: In graphite, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to 3 other carbon atoms in hexagonal planar layers.
The fourth valence electron of each carbon atom is delocalised across the hexagonal sheets, acting as mobile charge carriers.
In diamond, each carbon forms 4 strong covalent bonds in a rigid tetrahedral structure; all valence electrons are localised in single bonds, leaving no mobile charge carriers.
solution.finalAnswer: Each carbon in graphite forms 3 covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom
solution.commonTrap: Suggesting graphite conducts between layers rather than along/within the layers, or claiming graphite has mobile ions.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes metallic bonding in copper metal?
options: Electrostatic attraction between positive metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons
Shared pairs of electrons between adjacent metal atoms
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Weak van der Waals forces between neutral metal atoms
questions.correctAnswer: Electrostatic attraction between positive metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons

solution.formulaSetup: Standard Cambridge O-Level / IP definition of metallic bonding.
steps: Metals shed their outermost valence electrons into a shared electron cloud ('sea of delocalised electrons').
The bonding consists of the strong electrostatic attraction between the positively charged metal ions (cations) and this sea of delocalised electrons.
solution.finalAnswer: Electrostatic attraction between positive metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons
solution.commonTrap: Stating attraction between 'metal atoms' and electrons instead of 'positive metal cations'.

questions.questionText: Why does chlorine gas ($Cl_2$) have a very low boiling point ($-34^\circ\text{C}$)?
options: Little energy is required to overcome the weak intermolecular van der Waals forces between molecules
The covalent bond between chlorine atoms is very weak
Chlorine molecules are easily ionised into chloride ions
Chlorine has a low relative atomic mass
questions.correctAnswer: Little energy is required to overcome the weak intermolecular van der Waals forces between molecules

solution.formulaSetup: State changes in simple molecular structures involve overcoming intermolecular forces, NOT covalent bonds.
steps: $Cl_2$ has a simple covalent molecular structure.
During boiling, the strong intramolecular covalent bonds between chlorine atoms remain intact.
Only the weak intermolecular van der Waals forces between $Cl_2$ molecules are overcome.
Because these forces are weak, little thermal energy is needed, resulting in a low boiling point.
solution.finalAnswer: Little energy is required to overcome the weak intermolecular van der Waals forces between molecules
solution.commonTrap: Saying 'covalent bonds between atoms are broken during boiling' — a classic zero-mark misconception.

questions.questionText: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed between aluminium ($Al$, Group 13) and oxygen ($O$, Group 16)?
options: $AlO$
$AlO_2$

solution.formulaSetup: Cation: $Al^{3+}$. Anion: $O^{2-}$. Total net charge must equal zero.
steps: Aluminium loses 3 valence electrons: $Al \to Al^{3+} + 3e^-$.
Oxygen gains 2 valence electrons: $O + 2e^- \to O^{2-}$.
To balance charges: $2 \times (+3) + 3 \times (-2) = +6 - 6 = 0$.
Empirical formula is $Al_2O_3$.
solution.commonTrap: Inverting subscripts to $Al_3O_2$.

questions.questionText: Magnesium oxide ($MgO$) has a melting point of $2852^\circ\text{C}$, whereas sodium chloride ($NaCl$) has a melting point of $801^\circ\text{C}$. Why is the melting point of $MgO$ much higher?
options: $Mg^{2+}$ and $O^{2-}$ have higher ionic charges than $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$, resulting in stronger electrostatic attraction
$MgO$ has a giant covalent structure whereas $NaCl$ is ionic
Magnesium has more delocalised electrons than sodium
Oxygen has a smaller atomic radius than chlorine
questions.correctAnswer: $Mg^{2+}$ and $O^{2-}$ have higher ionic charges than $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$, resulting in stronger electrostatic attraction

solution.formulaSetup: Lattice energy is proportional to $\frac{q_1 q_2}{r_1 + r_2}$ (product of ionic charges over internuclear distance).
steps: Both $MgO$ and $NaCl$ have giant ionic lattice structures.
In $MgO$, ions carry charges of $+2$ and $-2$ (product of charges $= 4$).
In $NaCl$, ions carry charges of $+1$ and $-1$ (product of charges $= 1$).
Additionally, $Mg^{2+}$ and $O^{2-}$ have smaller ionic radii than $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$.
The electrostatic attraction between $Mg^{2+}$ and $O^{2-}$ is much stronger, requiring significantly more thermal energy to overcome.
solution.finalAnswer: $Mg^{2+}$ and $O^{2-}$ have higher ionic charges than $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$, resulting in stronger electrostatic attraction
solution.commonTrap: Falsely claiming $MgO$ is covalent because of its extraordinarily high melting point.

questions.questionText: Why are pure metals malleable and ductile, whereas giant ionic salts shatter (are brittle) when struck with a hammer?
options: In metals, layers of cations can slide over each other without breaking metallic bonds; in ionic salts, sliding brings like charges together causing repulsion
Metals have flexible covalent bonds; ionic salts have weak bonds
Ionic salts have mobile electrons that repel each other
Metals have empty spaces between atoms that absorb the impact
questions.correctAnswer: In metals, layers of cations can slide over each other without breaking metallic bonds; in ionic salts, sliding brings like charges together causing repulsion

solution.formulaSetup: Comparison of mechanical properties based on bonding models.
steps: In pure metals, orderly layers of positive metal cations can slide over each other without disrupting the non-directional sea of delocalised electrons.
In an ionic lattice, when a shear force is applied, layers of ions slide, bringing ions of the SAME charge next to each other (e.g., $Na^+$ next to $Na^+$, $Cl^-$ next to $Cl^-$).
The resulting strong electrostatic repulsion shatters the crystal lattice, making it brittle.
solution.finalAnswer: In metals, layers of cations can slide over each other without breaking metallic bonds; in ionic salts, sliding brings like charges together causing repulsion
solution.commonTrap: Failing to mention 'like charges are brought together causing repulsion' for ionic brittleness.

questions.questionText: An alloy of copper and zinc (brass) is much harder and less malleable than pure copper. What is the structural reason for this?
options: Zinc atoms have a different size, disrupting the regular layers of copper atoms and preventing them from sliding easily
Zinc forms strong ionic bonds with copper
Zinc removes the delocalised electrons from copper
Zinc forms a protective oxide layer that resists deformation
questions.correctAnswer: Zinc atoms have a different size, disrupting the regular layers of copper atoms and preventing them from sliding easily

solution.formulaSetup: Alloy hardness explanation in O-Level Chemistry syllabus.
steps: Pure copper consists of orderly, identical layers of copper cations that easily slide over one another when stress is applied.
Zinc atoms have a different atomic radius from copper atoms.
Introducing zinc disrupts the orderly arrangement and regularity of the lattice layers.
More force is required for the layers to slide over one another, making the alloy harder and less malleable.
solution.finalAnswer: Zinc atoms have a different size, disrupting the regular layers of copper atoms and preventing them from sliding easily
solution.commonTrap: Claiming chemical bonds are formed between copper and zinc (alloys are physical mixtures/solutions of elements, not new chemical compounds).

questions.questionText: Which of the following compounds contains BOTH ionic and covalent bonds?
options: Ammonium chloride ($NH_4Cl$)
Methane ($CH_4$)
Calcium chloride ($CaCl_2$)
Water ($H_2O$)
questions.correctAnswer: Ammonium chloride ($NH_4Cl$)

solution.formulaSetup: Identify compounds containing polyatomic ions.
steps: $NH_4Cl$ consists of ammonium cations ($NH_4^+$) and chloride anions ($Cl^-$) held together by ionic bonds in a crystal lattice.
Within each ammonium cation ($NH_4^+$), the nitrogen atom is bonded to 4 hydrogen atoms via covalent bonds (including one dative coordinate bond).
Therefore, $NH_4Cl$ contains both ionic and covalent bonding.
solution.finalAnswer: Ammonium chloride ($NH_4Cl$)
solution.commonTrap: Assuming all salts only have ionic bonds, overlooking polyatomic ions like $NH_4^+, SO_4^{2-}, NO_3^-, CO_3^{2-}$.

questions.questionText: Why is diamond extremely hard and has a very high melting point ($>3500^\circ\text{C}$)?
options: Each carbon atom is tetrahedrally bonded to 4 other carbons by strong covalent bonds in a rigid 3D lattice
Diamond has extremely strong electrostatic forces between carbon ions
Diamond has a sea of delocalised electrons holding atoms tightly
Diamond has heavy intermolecular forces between macromolecules
questions.correctAnswer: Each carbon atom is tetrahedrally bonded to 4 other carbons by strong covalent bonds in a rigid 3D lattice

solution.formulaSetup: Giant covalent network structure of diamond.
steps: Diamond has a giant covalent macromolecular structure.
Every carbon atom is covalently bonded to 4 other carbon atoms in a continuous, rigid 3D tetrahedral network.
Breaking this rigid network requires breaking a massive number of strong C-C covalent bonds, which requires an enormous amount of thermal/mechanical energy.
solution.finalAnswer: Each carbon atom is tetrahedrally bonded to 4 other carbons by strong covalent bonds in a rigid 3D lattice
solution.commonTrap: Referring to 'intermolecular forces' in diamond (there are NO separate molecules, hence no intermolecular forces).

questions.questionText: What type of bonding and structure does iodine ($I_2$) possess at room temperature, and what holds the crystal lattice together?
options: Simple molecular structure held by weak intermolecular van der Waals forces
Giant covalent lattice held by strong covalent bonds
Giant ionic lattice held by electrostatic attraction
Metallic structure held by delocalised electrons
questions.correctAnswer: Simple molecular structure held by weak intermolecular van der Waals forces

solution.formulaSetup: Group 17 halogens at room temperature.
steps: Iodine exists as diatomic molecules ($I_2$) where iodine atoms share a pair of electrons in a strong covalent bond.
In the solid state, $I_2$ forms a face-centred molecular crystal lattice.
The crystal is held together solely by weak intermolecular forces (induced dipole-dipole / van der Waals forces).
Because these intermolecular forces are weak, iodine readily sublimes upon gentle warming into purple vapor.
solution.finalAnswer: Simple molecular structure held by weak intermolecular van der Waals forces
solution.commonTrap: Thinking solid iodine is a giant covalent structure because it is a solid at room temperature.

questions.questionText: Why does aqueous hydrogen chloride ($HCl$) conduct electricity, whereas liquid hydrogen chloride ($HCl$) does not?
options: $HCl$ ionises in water into mobile $H^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions, whereas liquid $HCl$ consists only of neutral covalent molecules
Water provides free electrons that conduct electricity
Liquid $HCl$ forms an insulating ionic lattice
Water oxidises chlorine to form mobile chlorate ions
questions.correctAnswer: $HCl$ ionises in water into mobile $H^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions, whereas liquid $HCl$ consists only of neutral covalent molecules

solution.formulaSetup: Acid behavior: $HCl(g) + H_2O(l) \to H_3O^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq)$.
steps: Pure liquid $HCl$ is composed of discrete, neutral covalent molecules held by dipole-dipole forces; with no mobile ions or electrons, it cannot conduct electricity.
When dissolved in water, polar water molecules induce complete ionisation: $HCl(aq) \to H^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq)$.
The resulting mobile hydrogen and chloride ions are free to move and carry electric charge.
solution.finalAnswer: $HCl$ ionises in water into mobile $H^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions, whereas liquid $HCl$ consists only of neutral covalent molecules
solution.commonTrap: Assuming pure liquid $HCl$ is an ionic liquid like molten $NaCl$.

questions.questionText: How many shared pairs of electrons (covalent bonds) and how many unshared pairs (lone pairs) are present on the nitrogen atom in an ammonia molecule ($NH_3$)?
options: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair
3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs
2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs
4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs
questions.correctAnswer: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair

solution.formulaSetup: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons (Group 15). Each hydrogen contributes 1 valence electron.
steps: Nitrogen shares 1 electron with each of the 3 hydrogen atoms to form 3 single covalent bonds (3 bonding pairs).
Remaining valence electrons on nitrogen: $5 - 3 = 2$ non-bonding electrons.
2 non-bonding electrons form 1 lone pair.
Total: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair (giving a trigonal pyramidal geometry).
solution.finalAnswer: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair
solution.commonTrap: Confusing total lone electrons (2) with lone pairs (1).

questions.questionText: Substance $X$ has a melting point of $1410^\circ\text{C}$, does not conduct electricity when solid or molten, and is insoluble in water. What is the most likely identity and structure of $X$?
options: Silicon ($Si$), giant covalent structure
Sodium chloride ($NaCl$), giant ionic lattice
Magnesium ($Mg$), giant metallic lattice
Poly(ethene), macromolecular polymer
questions.correctAnswer: Silicon ($Si$), giant covalent structure

solution.formulaSetup: Deduce structure from physical properties: high m.p. ($>1000^\circ\text{C}$), non-conductor in both solid AND liquid state, insoluble.
steps: High melting point eliminates simple molecular substances (e.g. polyethene).
Non-conductor in the molten state eliminates giant ionic substances ($NaCl$ conducts when molten) and giant metallic substances ($Mg$ conducts in all states).
Giant covalent network (macromolecule) has high melting point and non-conducting properties in both solid and molten states.
Silicon ($Si$) forms a diamond-like giant covalent network with melting point $1410^\circ\text{C}$.
solution.finalAnswer: Silicon ($Si$), giant covalent structure
solution.commonTrap: Choosing $NaCl$ without noticing the condition 'does not conduct electricity when molten'.

questions.questionText: Explain why the boiling point of ethanol ($CH_3CH_2OH$, $78^\circ\text{C}$) is significantly higher than that of propane ($C_3H_8$, $-42^\circ\text{C}$), despite having similar relative molecular masses ($M_r = 46$ vs $44$).
options: Ethanol molecules can form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds via the $-OH$ group, whereas propane only possesses weak van der Waals forces
Ethanol has stronger covalent C-O and O-H bonds that break during boiling
Propane is a non-polar gas that decomposes upon heating
Ethanol is an ionic liquid at room temperature
questions.correctAnswer: Ethanol molecules can form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds via the $-OH$ group, whereas propane only possesses weak van der Waals forces

solution.formulaSetup: Intermolecular forces comparison between molecules of comparable $M_r$.
steps: Both ethanol ($M_r = 46$) and propane ($M_r = 44$) have simple molecular structures.
Ethanol possesses a highly electronegative oxygen atom bonded to hydrogen ($-OH$), enabling the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
Hydrogen bonds are substantially stronger than the instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (van der Waals) forces found between non-polar propane molecules.
Much more thermal energy is needed to overcome hydrogen bonds between ethanol molecules, giving it a much higher boiling point.
solution.finalAnswer: Ethanol molecules can form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds via the $-OH$ group, whereas propane only possesses weak van der Waals forces
solution.commonTrap: Claiming covalent bonds within the ethanol molecule break during boiling.

questions.questionText: Graphene is a single 2D layer of carbon atoms. Which combination of properties correctly describes graphene?
options: High electrical conductivity, exceptionally high tensile strength, single atom thickness
Insulator, brittle, transparent
Low melting point, poor conductor, ductile
Conducts only when dissolved, ionic lattice
questions.correctAnswer: High electrical conductivity, exceptionally high tensile strength, single atom thickness

solution.formulaSetup: Structure and advanced properties of graphene.
steps: Graphene is a 2D monolayer of carbon atoms arranged in an $sp^2$ hexagonal honeycomb lattice.
Electrical conductivity: Each carbon has 1 delocalised electron that moves freely across the 2D sheet, granting extremely high electrical conductivity.
Mechanical strength: Strong in-plane covalent $C-C$ bonds make graphene one of the strongest materials known (high tensile strength).
Thickness: Exactly one carbon atom thick.
solution.finalAnswer: High electrical conductivity, exceptionally high tensile strength, single atom thickness
solution.commonTrap: Assuming graphene is an insulator like diamond or soft like bulk graphite.

questions.questionText: Why is calcium fluoride ($CaF_2$) insoluble in water, whereas calcium chloride ($CaCl_2$) is highly soluble?
options: The lattice energy of $CaF_2$ is much greater than that of $CaCl_2$ because $F^-$ has a much smaller ionic radius than $Cl^-$
$CaF_2$ has a giant covalent macromolecular structure
Fluoride ions repel water molecules strongly
$CaCl_2$ forms covalent bonds with water
questions.correctAnswer: The lattice energy of $CaF_2$ is much greater than that of $CaCl_2$ because $F^-$ has a much smaller ionic radius than $Cl^-$

solution.formulaSetup: Solubility of ionic salts involves competition between lattice energy (energy needed to break the lattice) and hydration enthalpy.
steps: Both $CaF_2$ and $CaCl_2$ are ionic compounds.
Fluoride ion ($F^-$) has a much smaller ionic radius than chloride ($Cl^-$).
The smaller internuclear distance between $Ca^{2+}$ and $F^-$ results in an exceptionally large lattice energy for $CaF_2$.
The hydration energy released when ions are surrounded by water is insufficient to overcome the massive lattice energy of $CaF_2$, rendering it insoluble.
solution.finalAnswer: The lattice energy of $CaF_2$ is much greater than that of $CaCl_2$ because $F^-$ has a much smaller ionic radius than $Cl^-$
solution.commonTrap: Claiming $CaF_2$ is covalent.

questions.questionText: In the solid state, carbon dioxide forms dry ice, which sublimes at $-78.5^\circ\text{C}$. In contrast, silicon dioxide ($SiO_2$) melts at $1710^\circ\text{C}$. Why is there such a massive difference in physical properties between these two Group 14 dioxides?
options: $CO_2$ consists of simple molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, while $SiO_2$ is a giant covalent macromolecular network
$CO_2$ is ionic while $SiO_2$ is metallic
Silicon is a metal and forms metallic bonds
The $C=O$ double bond is weaker than the $Si-O$ single bond
questions.correctAnswer: $CO_2$ consists of simple molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, while $SiO_2$ is a giant covalent macromolecular network

solution.formulaSetup: Structural contrast: Simple molecular vs Giant covalent network.
steps: Carbon forms strong $p\pi-p\pi$ double bonds with oxygen, creating stable, discrete linear $O=C=O$ molecules.
These discrete $CO_2$ molecules interact with each other via weak intermolecular van der Waals forces, requiring very little energy to separate (sublimes at $-78.5^\circ\text{C}$).
Silicon has larger $3p$ orbitals, making $p\pi-p\pi$ overlap with oxygen unfavorable; instead, silicon forms four single $\sigma$-bonds with oxygen atoms.
This creates an infinite 3D giant covalent network where every $Si$ is bonded to $4$ oxygens and every $O$ to $2$ silicons, requiring immense energy to break.
solution.finalAnswer: $CO_2$ consists of simple molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, while $SiO_2$ is a giant covalent macromolecular network
solution.commonTrap: Stating that $C=O$ bonds are broken during sublimation of dry ice.

questions.questionText: A white crystalline solid $Z$ melts at $801^\circ\text{C}$. In solid form, it has a density of $2.16\text{ g/cm}^3$. When molten, it undergoes electrolysis to produce a silvery metal at the cathode and a pungent greenish-yellow gas at the anode. What are the identities of the products?
options: Sodium metal at cathode, chlorine gas at anode
Chlorine gas at cathode, sodium metal at anode
Hydrogen gas at cathode, oxygen gas at anode
Sodium hydroxide at cathode, chlorine at anode
questions.correctAnswer: Sodium metal at cathode, chlorine gas at anode

solution.formulaSetup: Electrolysis of molten $NaCl$: Cathode: reduction of metal cation ($Na^+ + e^- \to Na(l)$); Anode: oxidation of halide anion ($2Cl^- \to Cl_2(g) + 2e^-$).
steps: Identify solid $Z$: $NaCl$ (melting point $801^\circ\text{C}$).
At cathode (negative electrode): $Na^+$ ions migrate and gain electrons (reduction): $Na^+ + e^- \to Na(l)$ (silvery liquid metal).
At anode (positive electrode): $Cl^-$ ions migrate and lose electrons (oxidation): $2Cl^- \to Cl_2(g) + 2e^-$ (greenish-yellow pungent gas).
Because it is MOLTEN (anhydrous, no water present), $H^+$ and $OH^-$ are absent, so $H_2$ and $O_2$ cannot form.
solution.finalAnswer: Sodium metal at cathode, chlorine gas at anode
solution.commonTrap: Confusing electrolysis of MOLTEN $NaCl$ with AQUEOUS $NaCl$ (where $H_2$ gas is discharged at the cathode instead of $Na$ metal).
